stories.headline: Sepulcher's paving preview lands, but its independent review hits a source-evidence gate
stories.summary: A playable Godot preview now includes four native-resolution paving crops, the real Operator and camera, and three comparison modes. The implementation was landed and archived, but its independent review has no verdict: a source-scope host check rejected four paths. A narrowly pinned recovery proposal is drafted, not approved or dispatched.
stories.body: The Sepulcher paving experiment advanced from instructions to a committed, playable comparison scene. The scene uses four 512-pixel crops, the real Operator and camera, and neutral, full-crop and deliberate repeat presentations. The implementation closeout reports Godot, crop, LFS and capture checks passed, and the task packet was archived. That is implementation progress, not independent review acceptance or production-art approval. The preserved independent review received no verdict after its pre-review host source-scope check rejected four paths missing from the historical task's explicit source list. A new source-scope attestation implementation/review pair is drafted/manual. It proposes an exact four-path exception that cannot activate before its own independently accepted PASS, then separate recovery of the original preserved review run. Host worktree and liveness status are not independently verified.
bullets: Playable native-quad scene and capture harness committed to main.
Implementation archived; independent technical review has no verdict.
Four-path source-scope attestation packets are draft/manual, not ready/auto.
Human approval for production art remains outstanding.

article.lead: Sepulcher Gardens now has a committed playable paving comparison, bringing its first experimental floor material into a real Operator-camera scene. But the technical review has stopped before a verdict because the historical task did not explicitly name four source paths.

sections.heading: From artwork to a playable comparison
sections.text: The new Godot scene places four native 512-pixel crops alongside a neutral floor and a deliberately repeated tile. Switching modes lets reviewers distinguish the quality of the original composition from visible repetition in gameplay.

sections.heading: Why the review stopped
sections.text: The implementation was landed and archived, with tests reported in its closeout. Its separate independent review was preserved without a verdict when a host check rejected four source-bearing paths outside the original packet's explicit scope. No PASS or art approval follows from the implementation landing.

sections.heading: A narrow recovery, not a shortcut
sections.text: A new draft/manual attestation pair proposes pinning exactly those four historical paths. Its exception would remain inactive until its own independent review earns canonical acceptance. Only then could the original preserved review be recovered separately.

insights.title: A playable scene is not an accepted asset
insights.explanation: The preview now exists in code, but neither its independent technical review nor the human visual approval has been completed. That separation protects the production asset pipeline.

insights.title: Review provenance is the new bottleneck
insights.explanation: The blocker is not a missing texture or game scene. It is the review system's inability to authenticate four historically omitted source paths without weakening its broader protections.

article.takeaway: Sepulcher's preview implementation landed; independent technical acceptance and production-art approval remain outstanding.
article.next_watch: Look for a properly authorized, independently accepted four-path attestation and then recovery of the original preserved review.

details.overview: Main contains the playable scene implementation, task closeout, and archive. A subsequent main commit documents a no-verdict review preflight and draft/manual recovery pair. Local review process, worktree retention and disk state are not independently observed.

stories.headline: Validator's second correction closes without a passing independent review
stories.summary: CUSTODIAN's cycle-2 paired-review validator correction was archived with a nonpassing review outcome. This is a documented closeout, not acceptance of the validator fix. Further remediation requires an explicit decision rather than treating the completed packet as a PASS.
stories.body: A new main-branch closeout commit records a nonpassing independent review for the second validator correction and archives the correction packet. The distinction matters: completing or archiving an implementation does not mean the independent reviewer accepted its safety behavior. The previous review had identified a retry path that could bypass validation evidence. The latest closeout does not establish that the flaw is resolved or the review accepted. The next action is to inspect the exact findings and decide on bounded human-directed remediation; no automatic third correction is implied.
bullets: Cycle-2 correction archived with nonpassing review outcome.

article.lead: CUSTODIAN's second attempt to repair a validator loophole has reached closeout, but not acceptance. The latest record explicitly calls the independent review nonpassing, keeping the safety gate unresolved.

sections.heading: Closeout does not mean approval

sections.heading: The decision moves back to the findings
sections.text: The prior review showed that retrying after synchronization could bypass required validation evidence. The exact latest findings must be inspected before choosing another bounded repair; a third automatic correction should not be assumed.

insights.title: The review boundary held
insights.explanation: A completed implementation did not silently become an accepted fix. The independent review's nonpassing disposition remains visible and consequential.

article.takeaway: Cycle-2 correction closeout is verified; independent acceptance is not.

stories.headline: A second review catches a retry loophole in CUSTODIAN's safety gate
stories.summary: An independent review of the first validator correction found R1-01: a retry could land code after a main-branch merge without consuming a required after-sync validation report. The finding is recorded and a second correction/review pair is declared ready/auto. No cycle-2 implementation or PASS is established.
stories.body: The first correction improved the source-sync witness checks, but its independent reviewer reproduced a separate bypass: a finish attempt synchronizes main and pauses for validation, then a retry with an invalid report can land when the next sync returns unchanged. Cycle-1 review outcome is findings, not acceptance. Two new cycle-2 packets declare ready/auto, each with sequential prerequisites. Canonical dispatch, execution, passing review, and host teardown are unverified.
bullets: Cycle-1 independent review reproduced the invalid after-sync retry bypass R1-01.
Cycle-2 correction and paired review declare ready/auto; dispatch and acceptance are not proven.

article.lead: CUSTODIAN's review safeguards have uncovered a second flaw while trying to close the first. A reviewer showed that a retry could slip past validation after synchronizing with newer main-branch code, so the previous correction has findings rather than independent acceptance.

sections.heading: The dangerous second attempt
sections.text: The first finish attempt correctly pauses after merging newer main code. On retry, however, the merge is no longer new. The existing implementation checks the required validation report only when that invocation sees a changed merge. The reviewer reproduced a finish that accepted a false report by never examining it.

sections.heading: A second correction is prepared
sections.text: The archived cycle-1 review preserves finding R1-01. A new implementation packet and a separate independent-review packet are now declared ready for automatic handoff. They are sequential, not evidence that the repair is already running or accepted.

insights.title: A green test suite did not cover the retry
insights.explanation: The review's selected validation checks passed, but the missing retry scenario still allowed an invalid finish. This is a concrete gap between passing tests and a trustworthy lifecycle gate.

insights.title: The next fix must remember what happened before retry
insights.explanation: The new packet requires the pending synchronized tree and its validation report to remain bound across retries, including when the latest synchronization reports no change.

article.takeaway: The original provenance correction is not independently accepted; a second, narrower correction is ready to address the newly reproduced bypass.
article.next_watch: Look for the cycle-2 implementation landing, a regression proving invalid retries fail, and an independent PASS receipt.

article.takeaway: Source handoff is documented; gameplay validation and art acceptance are still separate, unfinished gates.

stories.headline: CUSTODIAN adopts a safer end-of-turn rule for temporary developer checkouts
stories.summary: A new repository policy requires every Codex turn to inventory its worktrees and either safely retire a disposable checkout or record why it must remain. It explicitly protects ignored files, live claims, private proof and uncertain owners. This is a policy landing, not evidence that any worktrees were removed.
stories.body: The new AGENTS and lifecycle documentation require branch SHA verification, tracked/untracked/ignored inventory, and use of supported finish or checkpoint commands when safe. The rule seeks to reduce accumulating temporary checkouts without sacrificing unique evidence or protected reviews. No current host worktree counts, disk measurements, or actual cleanup were inspected.
bullets: Turn-end worktree retention must now be justified by inspected evidence.
No actual checkout retirement or disk recovery is established by the policy commit.

article.lead: CUSTODIAN has changed the default treatment of temporary development checkouts. Instead of letting each Codex session leave a worktree behind indefinitely, the new rule requires a safe retirement decision at every handoff.

sections.heading: Cleanup must not destroy evidence
sections.text: A remote Git branch preserves committed tracked files, not ignored artwork, local caches, private captures or untracked proof. The new instructions require an inventory and exact remote SHA verification before a checkout can be removed.

sections.heading: A policy is not a cleanup report
sections.text: Finished work should use the canonical finish lifecycle; safely parked work can use checkpoint-and-remove. Protected reviews, unknown owners, dirty files and manual experiments must be retained when their safety cannot be proven. No host-level cleanup is verified by this documentation change.

insights.title: The bottleneck is safe retirement, not deletion
insights.explanation: The policy addresses storage growth without treating missing branches or absent worktrees as proof of successful closeout. Durable evidence and lifecycle state remain separate.

article.takeaway: A safer checkout-retirement rule is now documented, but actual worktree counts and disk recovery still require host evidence.
article.next_watch: Look for an exact host inventory showing created, retired, retained and total worktrees with verified remote SHAs.

stories.headline: Independent review finds a provenance loophole; corrective packets enter the dispatch queue
stories.summary: An independent validator-recertification review recorded blocking finding R0-01: the finish-time producer guard accepts some merge witnesses that the canonical consumer would reject. A narrowly scoped correction and independent review are now marked ready/auto, but neither has been executed or accepted.
stories.body: The reviewer documented R0-01 and archived the review with outcome findings, not PASS. Two follow-up packets now declare ready/auto with sequential dependencies. They are not proof of dispatcher eligibility or execution. The fix must reproduce the failure, strengthen producer-side witness validation without weakening the consumer, then receive a separate independent review.
bullets: A verified blocking review finding has a defined corrective path, not an accepted fix.
Watch for a canonical dispatch/claim, reproducible regression tests, implementation landing and independent PASS for the correction.

article.lead: A fresh independent review caught a mismatch in CUSTODIAN's review-evidence safeguards. One validator accepts weaker proof of a source-sync merge than the other, so the new guard cannot yet be trusted as an equivalent pre-publication check.

sections.heading: What the reviewer found
sections.text: Finding R0-01 identifies a producer-side check that can accept a changed-sync witness without the unique matching checkpoint event and other structural evidence required by the canonical consumer. The archived review explicitly records findings rather than acceptance.

sections.heading: A bounded correction is prepared
sections.text: The correction packet and its paired independent review were added and then switched from draft/manual to ready/auto. The correction must reproduce the failure and align the producer with the existing stronger consumer, not relax the consumer to pass tests.

insights.title: The weak point is before publication
insights.explanation: The consumer already demands stronger provenance; the gap is that the producer may let inadequate evidence reach that later check. Fixing the earlier gate reduces invalid review handoffs.

insights.title: Ready is not accepted
insights.explanation: Both new packets have declared readiness, but their dependencies, execution, tests and independent review still need separate evidence.

article.takeaway: A verified blocking review finding has a defined corrective path, not an accepted fix.
article.next_watch: Watch for a canonical dispatch/claim, reproducible regression tests, implementation landing and independent PASS for the correction.

article.lead: Sepulcher Gardens has a more exact way to test its first paving image in-game. The new brief replaces arbitrary resizing with four fixed native-resolution crops and asks for a comparison inside a scene using the actual Operator and camera.

sections.heading: A test designed to expose, not conceal, repetition
sections.text: The proposed three views distinguish a neutral blockout, a native four-crop mosaic, and a repeated northwest crop. That should reveal how the original texture reads at gameplay scale without claiming it already tiles seamlessly.

sections.heading: The missing physical handoff
sections.text: The source exists as an authoring artifact, but its presence on the Codex host or in Dropbox is not established. The brief requires matching its SHA-256 before work starts and forbids replacing it with a lookalike.

insights.title: Exact pixels make comparisons reproducible
insights.explanation: Pinned crops and a hash remove artistic discretion from the preview build, making any observed difference attributable to the chosen image arrangement rather than resampling.

insights.title: A playable preview is not an art approval
insights.explanation: The scene can inform the decision while the original paving still fails its seamless-repeat gate. Asset V2 intake remains separate.

article.takeaway: The preview design is specified, but the source transfer, playable build and art approval remain outstanding.

stories.headline: Sepulcher Gardens' first modular paving candidate looks promising, but fails its repeatability gate
stories.summary: The first paving image in CUSTODIAN's four-source environment-art experiment has received a technical review. Its stonework and weathering are promising, but visible repeated motifs and unproven seamless edges prevent approval. The source remains outside the production asset pipeline while a targeted correction is considered.
stories.body: A new main-branch art-review record documents one generated paving candidate for the Sepulcher Gardens modular pilot. The image is 1254×1254 rather than the planned 512×512 source, and its repeated 3×3 preview exposes recognizable dark-block and bronze L-shaped patterns. Diagnostic boundary measurements do not establish seamlessness. The review explicitly records technical correction needed and human approval pending. No Dropbox upload, Asset V2 ingest, or second pilot asset is documented. The original is a conversation artifact, not a public image; no screenshot is included. Main source: 44c07109a34e2a3935265a5127e2f1962a310031. Repository validation passed for this commit; this is not an art acceptance or gameplay integration.
bullets: One paving candidate generated; zero approved sources within the four-source pilot manifest.

article.lead: Sepulcher Gardens has its first candidate for a more flexible, modular floor-art approach. The stonework holds up as a visual direction, but the image cannot yet become a game-ready repeating surface: recognizable patterns repeat too conspicuously, and its edges have not passed a seamlessness check.

sections.heading: A promising material, not yet a usable tile
sections.text: The proposed paving combines weathered limestone, dark basalt and restrained bronze accents. A technical review found the detailed texture compelling, but a 3×3 preview at the intended 512-pixel size exposed recurring dark blocks and L-shaped bronze marks. The generated original is 1254 pixels square, so the target-size version still needs proper treatment.

sections.heading: Why repetition matters in play
sections.text: A single attractive image can become a visible stamp when laid across a walkable floor. That would make Sepulcher Gardens feel patterned by its asset boundaries rather than by the environment. The review recommends fixing the repeat seam and reserving bold bronze geometry for a separate overlay, instead of discarding the useful texture detail.

insights.title: The first bottleneck is repetition, not artistic direction
insights.explanation: The review praises the stonework while identifying specific tiling faults. That narrows the next experiment to a technical correction rather than an indiscriminate redraw.

insights.title: Approval remains a separate gate
insights.explanation: The manifest records one generated candidate and no approved sources. Neither the source image nor the diagnostic preview has entered the production asset pipeline, so the four-source pilot has not advanced to its second asset.

article.takeaway: The modular-art experiment has produced a reviewable first candidate, but not an approved floor asset. Its next useful result is a corrected repeat test and an explicit human decision.
article.next_watch: Look for a true 512-pixel 3×3 seam/repetition check and individual art approval before any overlay generation or Asset V2 handoff.

stories.headline: Sepulcher Gardens gets a four-asset experiment to test a more flexible environment art style
stories.summary: A new reversible design proposes testing a tiled floor, damage overlay, civic inlay and wall module with the real Operator in a sandbox. The plan could reduce reliance on single large AI-painted maps, but no images, playable test or approval are delivered.
stories.body: Main commit 796c32b0 adds a proposed four-source modular Sepulcher pilot, including a 1024×768 sandbox, 32px walkability grid, exact image prompts and proposed Asset V2 identities. The experiment compares a composed modular environment with the existing approach using the real Operator. It is explicitly planning only: not art generation authorization, registered assets, a runnable Godot scene, independent review or production cutover. Main at inspection: 7eaf776dfe57b971069262925275331bb78c7dbc. Full dispatcher audit and host state were not available.
bullets: Art owner: review the four-source experiment before authorizing image generation.
Gameplay owner: only after individual art approval, create an isolated Operator A/B sandbox without changing production scenes.

article.lead: Sepulcher Gardens may not need to be painted as one enormous image. A newly landed experiment proposes building a small playable scene from four independently reviewable art sources, then comparing the result with the existing full-environment approach. The proposal is concrete, but it has not yet produced art or gameplay.

sections.heading: Four pieces, one test scene
sections.text: The proposed ingredients are repeatable paving, a sparse damage overlay, a distinctive civic inlay and a separate wall module. They would be composed on a 1024×768 sandbox using a 32px grid and the real Operator, with movement and collision authored separately from the images.

sections.heading: A reversible test, not a redesign
sections.text: The experiment deliberately leaves the existing Gardens map, grave-event logic and production art queue untouched. Its acceptance gates require individual source review, seam and scale checks, and a side-by-side playable comparison before anyone considers a wider change.

insights.title: Separating art from geometry could make iteration cheaper
insights.explanation: If a floor texture can repeat cleanly while walls and walkability remain independent, adjusting a room may no longer require repainting an entire environment. The pilot is designed to test that possibility, not assume it.

insights.title: A real Operator comparison is the decisive gate
insights.explanation: A beautiful isolated tile is not enough. The proposed sandbox tests visual scale, readability, navigation and composition in the actual gameplay camera, where an art approach must ultimately succeed.

article.takeaway: A bounded modular-art experiment is documented on main; generation, approval, implementation and A/B results remain outstanding.
article.next_watch: Watch for explicit authorization and independently reviewed source images, followed by a real Operator sandbox comparison.

stories.headline: Review closeout gains a stronger safety guard as a stranded-review recovery packet becomes ready
stories.summary: A new main-branch runner guard authenticates the original reviewer session before allowing a committed PASS to close. A separate P0 supersession implementation and its paired review were marked ready for automatic dispatch. Neither change proves the protected review was accepted or that an executor started.
stories.body: Commit 7e965f88 landed a fail-closed review closeout guard with a reported 274 runner tests passing. Its attached summary explicitly preserves the protected original review in HOLD after a required profile dependency failure; the local status in that summary is historical, not freshly verified host state. Commit 7eaf776d changes the new unaccepted-supersession implementation and paired review packets from draft/manual to ready/auto. Their dependencies still apply; ready is not claimed or running. Full canonical dispatcher audit and independent review acceptance were not inspected.
bullets: Dispatcher owner: verify prerequisite review-agent-legacy-claim-scoped-snapshot-v1 before any claim.
Review owner: independently assess the landed closeout guard and preserve the original protected HOLD.

article.lead: CUSTODIAN's review machinery has acquired another safeguard against prematurely closing a stranded review. A new guard checks the original reviewer evidence before treating a recorded PASS as authentic. Meanwhile, a separate recovery workstream has moved from draft to dispatch-ready, though neither step resolves the protected review on its own.

sections.heading: The PASS must belong to the actual review
sections.text: The landed guard ties a review outcome to its original session, continuation, evidence digests and claim identity. A contradictory verdict or unresolved required dependency must hold closeout rather than being treated as a successful review.

sections.heading: A recovery route is queued, not running
sections.text: The new P0 unaccepted-supersession implementation and paired review now say ready/auto. The implementation still depends on a separate legacy-claim snapshot review, and the paired review depends on the implementation. Those declarations are dispatch eligibility inputs, not proof that either job has started.

insights.title: A recorded PASS is not the same as an accepted PASS
insights.explanation: The guard addresses a subtle failure mode: authentic-looking archived output can coexist with missing dependencies or mismatched session evidence. Closing such a review would incorrectly unlock downstream work.

insights.title: Recovery can preserve history instead of rewriting it
insights.explanation: The new packet describes a supersession lifecycle for reviews that cannot be accepted. Its intended distinction is between retaining the old evidence and creating a separately reviewable path forward.

article.takeaway: The safety guard is landed and a recovery implementation is ready, but independent acceptance and protected-run recovery remain unverified.
article.next_watch: Verify the prerequisite snapshot review and watch for an actual dispatcher claim, implementation landing and independent review receipt.

stories.headline: Environment art gains a precise 'next set' command, starting with Sepulcher Gardens
stories.summary: A new main-branch manifest sequence makes 'generate the next set' select the earliest unfinished, individually approved art set. The initial CAL-01 target is one Sepulcher Gardens underlay, not a bulk batch. No image was generated or approved by this commit.
stories.body: Main commit 5ee4a63d1bfcabdd53d27ba2f1ad3f4f231663a5 adds ordered generation_sets and a command contract to the existing Hub/Sepulcher/Awakening manifest. The first initial set CAL-01 is one 1152×1408 Gardens underlay; CAL-02 is a separate 160×96 memorial slab only after CAL-01 human approval. The sequence must reconcile real approval and source receipts rather than trusting the JSON checkpoint. This is planning/dispatch documentation, not image generation, human acceptance, Dropbox delivery or Asset V2 integration. No canonical dispatcher audit or host state inspected.
bullets: Art owner: reconcile existing approved source receipts, then generate or present CAL-01 for individual review.

article.lead: CUSTODIAN's environment art plan now answers a practical question: what exactly should happen when someone says 'generate the next set'? A new ordered manifest chooses the first unfinished image set and requires real source and approval evidence before moving forward. The change is on main, but it has not produced a new image.

sections.heading: One command, one unambiguous next target
sections.text: At the documented initial baseline, CAL-01 calls for a single 1152×1408 Sepulcher Gardens environment underlay. Its successor, CAL-02, is a 160×96 memorial slab, but only after the first source is individually approved. Later sets can contain two distinct images where style and geometry permit.

sections.heading: The queue cannot outrun review
sections.text: The selection rule checks real approved-source hashes, review receipts and asset intake before relying on a stored checkpoint. If an image is already generated but awaits approval, the next command returns to that review instead of skipping ahead or generating a duplicate.

insights.title: A conversational instruction becomes deterministic production
insights.explanation: The manifest now binds a common request to exact image identities, sizes and prompts, reducing ambiguity between a planning batch and an actual generation action.

insights.title: The approval gate is the real cursor
insights.explanation: Progress depends on individually verified human decisions, not on whether a manifest field says 'next'. This protects against duplicate generation and falsely completed art states.

article.takeaway: The next-art command is specified and ordered, but source generation, approval and runtime integration remain separate unverified milestones.
article.next_watch: Watch for a recoverable CAL-01 candidate and explicit individual human approval, with a source hash or receipt.

stories.headline: CUSTODIAN sets image-by-image approval rules before its large environment art push
stories.summary: A new main-branch protocol distinguishes planning batches from actual image generation. Large environments and seams stay one-at-a-time; small compatible props may be grouped after style calibration. Every asset still requires its own approval.
stories.body: Commit 91f44c89 adds the standing non-Operator AI art generation and review protocol and updates the art manifest guidance. It organizes queues of 5–10 states but requires individually reviewable sources, starts the five-image calibration one at a time, and only allows small compatible groups after style lock. This is guidance, not generated art or accepted runtime assets. Main 91f44c89e9a5bf9b269619d513777a403cc6530e.
bullets: Art owner: produce first calibration image with real neighboring references and seek individual approval.

article.lead: The planned Hub, Sepulcher and Awakening art program now has a practical production rulebook. Its central distinction is simple: organizing several images into a queue does not mean generating them as one collage or approving them as a group. The new protocol is on main, but it does not establish that any artwork has been produced.

sections.heading: Different art needs different treatment
sections.text: Large district underlays, connectors and animation states are generated individually because camera alignment, seams and frame continuity matter. Only small compatible props and decals may be grouped after a visual style has been approved, and each source remains independently reviewable.

sections.heading: The first five are a calibration gate
sections.text: The existing manifest's first five image states must be produced and approved one at a time. Approved neighboring art should guide each candidate. A source must then pass a separate asset-intake process before it can become a runtime asset.

insights.title: Batch planning is not batch approval
insights.explanation: A queue of 5–10 states is an organizational unit. The protocol prevents an attractive collage from being mistaken for independently accepted, correctly registered game art.

insights.title: Registration risk determines the batch size
insights.explanation: Images that touch existing geometry or neighboring scenery demand single-image attention. The rule protects level continuity while allowing limited efficiency for low-risk decorative pieces.

article.takeaway: Art production now has explicit review and batching boundaries, but image delivery and game integration remain unproven.
article.next_watch: The first individually approved calibration image and its source receipt.
